questions.prompt: Which OOP principle hides an object's internal state behind a controlled interface?
questions.explanation: Encapsulation bundles data with the methods that operate on it and restricts direct access, so the object can protect its own invariants. Abstraction, by contrast, hides complexity behind a simpler model.

options.text: Defining several methods with the same name but different parameters
A subclass providing its own implementation of a method inherited from a superclass
Calling a method before it is declared

questions.explanation: Overriding replaces inherited behaviour and is resolved at run time by the object's actual type, enabling polymorphism. Overloading, by contrast, varies the parameter list and is usually resolved at compile time.

questions.prompt: The Liskov Substitution Principle states that:

options.text: Every class must have exactly one parent
Objects of a subclass should be usable anywhere the superclass is expected, without breaking correctness

questions.explanation: A subtype must honour the contract of its base type so substituting it does not surprise callers. Violations, like a Square subclass of Rectangle that breaks width/height independence, are a classic warning sign.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between composition and inheritance?

options.text: Composition builds behaviour by holding other objects (has-a); inheritance derives from a base type (is-a)

questions.explanation: Composition assembles functionality from contained objects, giving looser coupling and more flexibility, which is why 'favour composition over inheritance' is common advice. Inheritance couples a subclass tightly to its parent's implementation.

questions.prompt: An abstract class differs from an interface (protocol) in that it:

options.text: Can hold state and provide partial implementations

questions.explanation: An abstract class shares fields and concrete methods with subclasses, but usually limits a type to one parent. An interface declares a contract that unrelated types can each adopt.

questions.prompt: Which design pattern ensures a class has only one instance with a global access point?
questions.explanation: The Singleton restricts construction so exactly one instance exists, used for shared resources like a configuration or logger. It is often criticised for introducing hidden global state.

questions.prompt: The Factory pattern is used to:

options.text: Create objects without exposing the concrete class to the caller

questions.explanation: A factory centralises object creation behind an interface, so callers depend on the abstraction rather than a specific implementation. This makes swapping concrete types easy.

questions.prompt: The Single Responsibility Principle says a class should:

options.text: Have only one reason to change

questions.explanation: A class focused on a single responsibility has one axis of change, making it easier to maintain and test. Mixing responsibilities means unrelated changes ripple into the same class.

questions.prompt: The Observer pattern establishes what kind of relationship?

options.text: A one-to-many notification, where subscribers are informed of a subject's changes

questions.explanation: One subject maintains a list of observers and pushes updates to all of them when its state changes, decoupling the source from the consumers. UI event systems are built on this pattern.

questions.prompt: What does runtime polymorphism depend on?

options.text: Dynamic dispatch that selects the method implementation from the object's actual type
The number of parameters a method has
The order in which classes are declared

questions.explanation: A virtual method call is resolved at run time using the object's real type, often via a vtable, so a base-type reference invokes the subclass override. Static methods are bound at compile time and are not polymorphic.
